j.learned_fact: Hot water makes steam, which fogs a mirror; hot taps can burn so don't touch.
j.thinking_skill: notices one cause and effect (hot water → steam); counts to three
j.notes: Three learning goals (steam, counting, hot-water safety) are stacked into a very short piece, so the counting line feels bolted on; little narrative tension or surprise.

j.learned_fact: A drum can be made of clay, and it makes a sound when you hit it.
j.thinking_skill: notices one cause and effect (hitting makes sound)
j.notes: Flat list of events with no problem or arc; the narrator's line "Miss Rosa works hard to serve her students" is an adult moralizing aside, and Aiden's cause-effect statement sounds scripted rather than childlike.

j.learned_fact: Four circles counted one by one make the number four; also the (odd) claim that a crayon colors sand and sun dries sand lighter.
j.thinking_skill: counts objects one-to-one to four
j.notes: The crayon-on-sand and "sun made them dry" bits are illogical and disconnected, and "I will invite you to draw with me" is stilted forced vocabulary; the story has no problem or arc beyond counting to four.

j.learned_fact: Painted wheels rolled across paper leave lines; the story also claims pushing harder makes darker lines and pushing fast makes longer lines — the speed claim is not true (line length depends on how far you push, not how fast).
j.thinking_skill: notices a simple cause and effect (push harder → darker line)
j.notes: Blue paint appears with no set-up after Hunter chose only red, and the "fast = long, slow = short" claim is false. Sequence words (First/Next/Then/Last) and the odd phrase "a true line of paint" feel bolted on.

j.learned_fact: Ants live outside in dirt and grass and come indoors looking for food crumbs — accurate; also sequence words first/next/then/last.
j.thinking_skill: asks where something came from and accepts an explanation
j.notes: Two loosely stitched episodes; the sequence words and the ant fact are delivered as explicit instruction, ending in a bolted-on moral line. Stella never reasons herself.

j.learned_fact: Sequence words (first, next, then, last) describe the steps of taking turns in a line; counting down as people leave the line (4 ahead, then 3).
j.thinking_skill: counts and updates a position in a line
j.notes: Reads like a checklist of targets (sequence words, counting, a rule, oddly bolted-on details like the "weak rail" and "did not frown"), with no real problem or tension; the social lesson is stated outright rather than dramatized.

j.learned_fact: One cup is half of two cups, so the butter is half the amount of flour — true but trivial; the implied claim that recipes generally work by such ratios is loose.
j.thinking_skill: recognizes a simple part-whole ratio (half)
j.notes: The "caring" theme is stated outright rather than shown ("I care about spending this time with you"), and the math/spoon lessons are delivered as grandma's mini-lectures; Easton never solves anything himself. Vocabulary sits below an 8-year-old's level.

j.learned_fact: Texts have different purposes — to sell, to inform, or to entertain; also that penguins live on ice in Antarctica and dive deeper than most birds.
j.thinking_skill: classifies items by purpose across a comparison chart
j.notes: It's a media-literacy lesson plan wearing a thin story costume: no conflict, no stakes, and the mother is a teacher prompt ("Tell me what you notice"). Maya reaches the "correct" answer instantly with no wrong guesses or discovery.

j.learned_fact: A grape sinks in fresh water but floats in salt water because dissolved salt makes water denser. The explanation that "the atoms and molecules in salt water are packed more tightly together" is misleading — density rises mainly because dissolved salt adds mass, not because water molecules pack tighter.
j.thinking_skill: offers an alternative explanation ("thicker") and tests a quantitative guess by asking
j.notes: Nearly all the science comes from Ms. Chen's explanations while Zoe mostly watches; the "half as heavy" question feels planted, and the density explanation is technically sloppy. Phrases like "almost steady and equal" are vague filler.

j.learned_fact: A midfielder connects defense and offense — the only concrete fact; the "crowd energy" insight is trivially obvious.
j.thinking_skill: notices a pattern and checks whether it holds for the rest of the game
j.notes: The "discovery" that crowds cheer when their team scores is banal and inflated into a life lesson, and the history-of-morale tangent feels bolted on; the tidy closing moral flattens an otherwise pleasantly observed first-date scene.

j.learned_fact: Baking soda + vinegar produce carbon dioxide gas, which leavens dough. FALSE detail: the story says the cup felt warm — this reaction is endothermic and actually feels cooler; also "atoms combining" is loose (molecules rearrange), and the baking history is vague/unsourced.
j.thinking_skill: varies one ingredient at a time and infers an unseen cause from observed effects
j.notes: Mostly narrated summary of a lesson rather than a scene: no obstacle, no dialogue beyond one line, and the last two paragraphs restate the moral twice. Contains a factual error (warm cup) and a hand-wavy history paragraph; also pitched a bit young for a 6th grader.

j.learned_fact: Removing one link in a food chain (grasshoppers) starves the consumers above it, while the producer below grows unchecked.
j.thinking_skill: traces a single cause-and-effect chain by covering one link
j.notes: The content (basic food chain) and the "aha" are well below a 12-year-old's level; a 7th grader would already know this, and real ecology (food webs, alternative prey, trophic cascades) is never touched. The kindly stranger buying supplies is a contrived device, and the "experiment" is just covering a card.

j.learned_fact: A teaching technique: asking a learner to explain their reasoning and to teach concepts back helps them catch their own errors. The "statistically more likely" claim is vague and unsupported as stated.
j.thinking_skill: changes one variable in her tutoring approach and observes the effect
j.notes: Almost entirely summary narration with no scenes, no dialogue beyond two lines, and no actual math shown; the lesson is stated repeatedly rather than dramatized. Theme fits a 13-year-old but the flat "she realized" reflection reads younger and duller than 9th-grade fiction.

j.learned_fact: That clear step-by-step instructions can reduce confusion and increase use of a service — demonstrated with a before/after count (19 vs 32 students). The genetics aside ("traits pass through families") is true but unsupported and irrelevant.
j.thinking_skill: makes one before/after comparison of a single changed variable (with no control for confounds)
j.notes: A bizarre non-sequitur paragraph about genetics is bolted in, and vocabulary words ("entail," "introduction") are forced; the theme is summarized in teacher-lecture dialogue rather than dramatized, and the flat, telling prose plus simplistic reasoning sit well below a 9th-grade reader.

j.learned_fact: Debugging means isolating an error by tracing code line by line and then changing one variable at a time to see its effect — e.g. swapping * for / produced absurdly large outputs, and extending the time period from 1 to 10 years multiplied accumulated erosion.
j.thinking_skill: isolates a single fault, then systematically varies one variable at a time to observe its effect
j.notes: The conflict (a single typo) is too trivial and the growth-mindset moral is stated outright by mentor and narrator rather than dramatized; for a 16-year-old the vocabulary, stakes and psychology are all under-pitched, and the erosion model stays vague. The line "errors that had seemed to flatter only her self-doubt" is garbled.

j.learned_fact: The intended lesson is that equal percentage discounts off different starting prices yield different final prices — but the story's own numbers contradict it: 12→8 is a 33% reduction, not 50%, so the resolution is mathematically false.
j.thinking_skill: weighs two competing explanations (error vs. intent) and separates evidence from assumption
j.notes: The central puzzle is resolved by an explanation that the story's own arithmetic disproves (12 to 8 is not 50% off), so the "mystery" is fake. Beyond that it is an essay about epistemic humility with a thin narrative skin, far below an 11th grader's thematic and conceptual range — a trivially small ethical stake and no real complication.

j.learned_fact: Variable names in code are case/character exact: 'water_usage' and 'waterusage' are two different identifiers; also that raw per-building water totals are confounded by building function (pool, kitchen).
j.thinking_skill: identifies a confounding variable and questions whether evidence supports a causal claim
j.notes: The story is mostly narrated summary and explicit moralizing—Marcus and Mr. Chen each deliver a speech restating the lesson, and the final paragraph spells it out again. Almost no scene, dialogue, or stakes; the confounding-variable insight is told rather than dramatized. (Minor slip: a mismatched variable name would usually be a NameError, plausible but the "crash every time" framing is thin.)

j.learned_fact: Confirmation bias: treating fear as evidence and reading meaning into ambiguity; the story misattributes this to a "logical fallacy their math teacher showed them" — it's a cognitive bias, and the description is vague.
j.thinking_skill: weighs two competing explanations and notices his own confirmation bias
j.notes: The closing paragraph abandons scene for a thesis statement on evidence vs. interpretation, and the mid-story metacognition is too tidily articulated to feel like real anxious thought; dialogue is scarce and the "lesson" is stated rather than dramatized.

j.learned_fact: A vague claim that "research showed" sustained attention has measurably declined while information access expanded — unsourced and contested; the main takeaway is the idea of dialectical rather than binary argument.
j.thinking_skill: holds two conflicting framings of technology in tension rather than resolving them
j.notes: Almost entirely interior summary-narration with no scene, dialogue, or stakes; the essayistic voice explains the theme rather than dramatizing it, and the "research showed" fact is generic and unverified.

j.learned_fact: That phone batteries contain cobalt that must be mined — the only concrete fact; everything else is abstract assertion about supply chains.
j.thinking_skill: reframes individual blame as systemic incentive structure
j.notes: Almost nothing happens; the last four paragraphs are essayistic narration restating the same thesis about systems in slightly different words. Specific knowledge (actual supply-chain facts, statistics) is gestured at but never delivered, so the reader learns a stance rather than content.

j.learned_fact: The literary-theory idea that meaning is co-created between author and reader rather than fixed by authorial intent (intentional fallacy / reader-response), though it's only gestured at, not named.
j.thinking_skill: weighs two competing explanations of where meaning resides and holds both
j.notes: Voice is charming but essayistic and repetitive; the "insight" is stated in abstract summary lines rather than dramatized, and nothing is at stake, so it reads more like a mood piece than a story. For a 12th-grade target the ideas stay introductory (no terms, texts, or real argument), and the narrator's quirk-heavy tone skews younger.
